Bishop's Hill fully demolished, no protests from residents

So said he received the demolition notice at the end of July and immediately reached out to Sham Shui Po district councillors, hoping to preserve the fitness equipment on Wozai Hill. However, he quoted their reply as saying "none of the equipment will be preserved." So noted that in previous instances of demolition, residents were able to organise petition campaigns to protest, but this time the notification period was so short that there was insufficient time to mobilise the community to stop the works. As a result, a morning exercise spot enjoyed by residents for over 20 years will soon be gone.

Three days ago (the 10th), the Home Affairs Department announced the Wozai Hill enhancement plan, under which the government will clear illegal and unsafe structures, facilities or miscellaneous items on the hill in phases, citing that these objects have been illegally occupying government land for years.

Yesterday (the 12th), at around 6:30 in the morning, staff from the Lands Department and uniformed police arrived on site, cordoning off the area from the foot to the top of the Tong Yam Street hillside rest garden. Movers then arrived to take away fitness equipment, bicycles, ping-pong tables and other items. Police deployed a冲锋车 and a prisoner transport vehicle as a precaution. So said this is just a place where residents exercise, and he does not understand the purpose of the police arrangement: "The officers are just standing there, watching the whole time. What are we doing now? Are we rioters? Have we broken the law?"

From "morning exercise hotspot" to LCSD facilities

So pointed out that residents crowdfunded a total of HK$400,000 to build the "morning exercise hotspot" on Bishop's Hill, which included a ping-pong table, fitness equipment, and unofficial hiking trails built decades ago. On the day of demolition, many residents were still doing morning exercises and using the fitness equipment. Several residents said they were deeply saddened by the disappearance of a place they had used for morning exercise for years. Some residents kept asking Mr So what to do, but Mr So himself did not know what to do.

He said he had spent several consecutive days moving the fitness equipment away, hoping to preserve as much of what he had built with his own hands as possible. Currently, he has removed all the muscle massage rollers, while some residents wish to relocate parts of the religious statues to Lantau Island.

According to the Home Affairs Department's Wozai Hill enhancement plan, the "morning exercise hotspot" will be converted into Leisure and Cultural Services Department facilities, and the "home-made" fitness equipment on the hill will be replaced with standard LCSD recreational equipment. As for the religious statues, religious leaders will be invited to the site to handle them appropriately.

Surviving against the odds: building Bishop's Hill "morning exercise hotspot"

75-year-old So Chi-keung is a SARS survivor. Due to side effects from medication, he suffered后遗症 such as muscle pain, weakness and fatigue. After three years of physiotherapy, his condition showed no improvement. In 2008, So was invited by a neighbour to visit Bishop's Hill. After doing morning exercises there, he found his spirits improved, which he attributed to the fresh air on the hill. He therefore began going to Bishop's Hill to exercise every morning at six o'clock. After persisting for a month, he regained his health and vitality, and decided to stop physiotherapy altogether.

In 2009, Mr So travelled to South Korea and was inspired by the local fitness facilities. After returning to Hong Kong, he used the designs as reference and "hand-made" exercise bikes and resistance machines at his own hardware factory. He single-handedly disassembled the equipment and transported the parts up Bishop's Hill, describing the manufacturing process as simple but the transport uphill as extremely arduous. It took him four years to build over 20 pieces of fitness equipment on Bishop's Hill, including swings, balance bars and rollers, which he placed on the vacant land above the current Sham Shui Po service reservoir. At the time, some elderly residents opposed him, but later, after neighbourhood residents used the equipment and found relief from physical ailments, the facilities became very popular.

Bishop's Hill exposed for the first time; residents protest against demolition

So said that in 2014, over 200 young people held a trance party on Bishop's Hill, causing a noise nuisance. When police arrived, they discovered for the first time a large number of privately-owned fitness facilities. Subsequently, the Water Supplies Department increased patrols of Bishop's Hill and repeatedly drove away residents using the equipment, and planned to demolish the facilities. At that time, Mr So organised several protest activities and went in person to the Sham Shui Po District Council Secretariat to fight for the retention of the fitness area.

Accidental viral moment: Bishop's Hill reservoir becomes a Grade 1 historic building

In 2017, the Water Supplies Department planned to clear the unauthorised structures on Bishop's Hill and return the land to the Lands Department. At the time, the roots of two large trees on top of the reservoir had extended into the structure, posing a risk of collapse. In 2020, with the removal of the trees and the filling-in of the reservoir about to proceed, the Water Supplies Department promised that Mr So's fitness facilities could be placed on the filled-in vacant land, and So agreed to the works.

As a result, on Christmas Eve, Mr So and a volunteer snuck into the reservoir to check for any items left behind, and took photographs that were posted on social media. The images attracted large crowds to visit and打卡 the reservoir, drawing public attention. So said that at the time, the public protested against demolishing the reservoir because of its historical value, and one regular Bishop's Hill visitor, Sister Fong, even stood in front of a drilling machine to stop the demolition works.

In 2021, the reservoir was assessed by the Antiquities Advisory Board as a Grade 1 historic building. The reservoir was preserved and opened to the public for visits, and Mr So relocated the fitness facilities to the foot of the hill.

The Mao Zedong statue incident may have triggered the demolition

In June 2022, the Sham Shui Po District Management Committee wanted to clear the shrines and fitness facilities. Mr So launched a petition to fight for their retention, stating that a total of 3,399 Sham Shui Po district residents signed, and he delivered the letter to the Home Affairs Department, pledging not to expand the facilities further.

So said that after this, Bishop's Hill remained peaceful, and the government did not indicate that it must clear the site. However, in early 2026, resident Sister Fong erected a Mao Zedong statue and a Mao Zedong Cultural Hall on Bishop's Hill. Although these were later removed, So believes the Mao Zedong incident rekindled the government's attention to Bishop's Hill. Combined with some residents making a great deal of noise on the hill and disturbing nearby residents, this led the government to decide on a complete clearance of Bishop's Hill.

In early 2026, resident Sister Fong set up a Mao Zedong statue and a Mao Zedong Cultural Hall on Bishop's Hill, reigniting controversy over the use of the hill. (File photo)

"Without Bishop's Hill, I would have lived 20 years less"

Watching workers dismantle the fitness equipment he had built one by one, So did not show grief. He plans to bring the equipment he has removed back to his ancestral home, and he keeps recounting the history of Bishop's Hill to the media. In fact, he is well aware that Bishop's Hill is highly controversial and that the "morning exercise hotspot" has been unauthorised for years, but he believes the place has benefited many residents. He hopes that by telling the story of Bishop's Hill, he can gain the government's recognition. Although ultimately the facilities were not preserved, he still wants to pass the story on, to repay Bishop's Hill for the grace it has shown him.

He bid farewell to Bishop's Hill: "I am grateful it gave me a new life. Without it, I wouldn't have had these 20 years—I should have died. If not for Bishop's Hill, I would have died... Moreover, I'm a SARS survivor who has suffered. Do you think I could have lived until today?"
